papers.abstract_en: Mitochondrial dysfunction drives diseases, including ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and inflammation. Conventional mitochondria-targeted strategies offer only partial rescue and are insufficient for severe, irreversible damage. Mitochondrial transplantation (MT)-the delivery of exogenously isolated functional mitochondria to injured cells-has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy that directly restores mitochondrial bioenergetic function and may subsequently modify the tissue microenvironment. This Review examines the entire MT pipeline, from mitochondrial source selection, isolation and preservation, to in vivo delivery strategies. We critically examine the multiple mechanisms underlying MT's therapeutic efficacy, including cellular uptake and intracellular integration, energy restoration and metabolic reprogramming, redox rebalancing, remodeling of mitochondrial quality control (fusion/fission, mitophagy, biogenesis), and immunomodulation. We summarize preclinical and clinical applications across multiple organ systems-heart, nervous system, liver, kidney, lung, skeletal muscle, retina-as well as in oncology and aging. We analyze five major translational bottlenecks: the lack of standardized manufacturing protocols, undefined dose-response relationships, immunogenicity and long-term safety uncertainties, the decisive impact of mitochondrial heterogeneity, and regulatory ambiguity. We outline future directions-mechanistic deepening, engineered target delivery, individualized mitochondrial medicine, combinatorial regimens, and a phased clinical roadmap. MT is not merely energy supplementation; it may reshape cellular metabolism, quality control networks, and immune microenvironments, representing a shift from pharmacological modulation of mitochondrial function toward organelle replacement strategies. Despite challenges, these advances may facilitate individualized mitochondrial therapies as a proposed future direction.

papers.abstract_en: UNLABELLED: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is the etiologic agent of a highly lethal hemorrhagic disease spread by ticks throughout Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, for which no FDA- or EMA-approved vaccines or therapeutics exist. A lack of fundamental understanding of the molecular mechanisms of CCHFV assembly, egress, and entry has challenged the development of medical countermeasures. Herein, we investigated the molecular basis of replicative efficacy of a highly protective recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine bearing the CCHFV glycoprotein complex (rVSV-GPC). We identified key amino acid residues associated with rVSV-GPC adaptation and showed that these could be transferred to a divergent CCHFV genetic background to afford a new vaccine vector with enhanced protective efficacy against heterologous viral challenge. We show that the key amino acid substitutions enhance rVSV-GPC infectivity via multiple distinct biochemical and cell-biological mechanisms. Our mechanistic studies provide the first evidence that SKI-1 cleavage at the GP38-Gn boundary modulates the pH threshold of CCHFV membrane fusion and points to a critical role for virion-associated GP38 and GP38-Gn interaction in regulating the pre-fusion conformation of the glycoprotein spike during virion biogenesis, egress, and cell entry. IMPORTANCE: Herein, we investigated the molecular basis of replicative efficacy of a highly protective rVSV-GPC vaccine candidate. We identified key amino acid residues associated with rVSV-GPC adaptation, including two novel residues, and showed that a minimal set of these could be transferred to a divergent CCHFV genetic background to afford a new vaccine vector with enhanced protective efficacy against heterologous viral challenge. Our work provides important new information to refine VSV-vectored CCHFV vaccines, to assess which critical GPC adaptations might benefit other vaccine modalities such as subunit and RNA, and to aid in the development of vaccines against divergent orthonairoviruses. Our findings also shed new light on the basic biology of CCHFV. We show that the key amino acid substitutions enhance rVSV-GPC infectivity via multiple, distinct biochemical and cell-biological mechanisms. Most notably, we provide the first evidence that SKI-1 cleavage at the GP38-Gn boundary modulates the pH threshold of viral membrane fusion. This points to an unanticipated role for virion-associated GP38 and GP38-Gn interaction in protecting and regulating the pre-fusion conformation of GPC during CCHFV biogenesis, egress, and cell entry.

papers.abstract_en: N-Myc interactor (NMI) functions in various viral infections and serves as a regulatory component of innate immune signaling, its function during bovine ephemeral fever virus (BEFV) infection remains to be elucidated. Herein, we establish that NMI attenuates BEFV replication in BHK-21 and MDBK cells, as evidenced by diminished viral nucleoprotein gene expression and viral loads in NMI-overexpressing cells, whereas NMI depletion significantly enhances viral replication. Further analyses reveal that NMI augments type I interferon (IFN-I) pathway activation via the transcriptional induction of Ifnb and downstream effectors, namely Isg15, Ifitm3, Mx1, Isg54 and Isg56. At the molecular level, NMI engages with IRF3, facilitating its phosphorylation and subsequent nuclear import, consequently potentiating IFN-I-mediated immune activation. Notably, BEFV infection counteracts this antiviral defense by inducing autophagy, resulting in time-dependent autophagic degradation of NMI. Further analysis demonstrates that BEFV-mediated NMI degradation occurs selectively through the autophagy receptor NIP3-like protein X (NIX), as pharmacological inhibition of autophagy or NIX knockout abrogates NMI degradation, while NIX overexpression accelerates NMI turnover. Collectively, our results delineate a novel molecular mechanism whereby NMI restricts BEFV replication through the IRF3-IFN axis, while BEFV evades this restriction via NIX-mediated selective autophagy. These observations furnish critical insights into NMI function and the dynamic crosstalk between host antiviral defenses and viral immune evasion mechanisms, which may lay the groundwork for the rational design of antiviral therapeutics.

papers.abstract_en: The Western diet (WD) is associated with skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism, redox imbalance and inflammation. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiome-derived metabolites contribute to host metabolic regulation, yet the role of Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids in skeletal muscle remains unknown. This study tested whether two structurally related bacterial glycine lipids, lipid 654 (L654) and lipid 1256 (L1256), regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial remodelling in WD-fed Ldlr-/- mice. Male Ldlr-/- mice were fed a normal chow or WD and administered L654, L1256 or vehicle control for 8 weeks. Skeletal muscle glycine lipid accumulation, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial biogenesis markers, mitophagy-associated signalling, inflammatory and antioxidant proteins and muscle fibre cross-sectional area were assessed. L1256, but not L654, accumulated in skeletal muscle. Functionally, L1256 selectively enhanced fatty acid-supported mitochondrial respiration and increased respiratory control ratio. L1256 also increased peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and electron transport chain complexes IV and V, suggesting enhanced oxidative mitochondrial remodelling. In parallel, L1256 altered markers associated with mitochondrial quality control signalling, increased nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), suppressed nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) signalling and preserved muscle fibre cross-sectional area. L654 upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis transcripts without altering protein abundance. These findings identify L1256 as a microbiome-derived lipid retained within skeletal muscle that enhanced oxidative metabolism and preserved mitochondrial quality signalling under metabolic stress. The data suggest that tissue retention of bacterial lipids may be an important determinant of skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation. KEY POINTS: Western diet contributes to skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism and chronic inflammation. Microbiome-derived glycine lipids are bioactive molecules from Bacteroidota species, but their effects on skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism remain poorly understood. Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids produce distinct skeletal muscle responses in Western diet-fed Ldlr- / - mice, where lipid 1256 accumulated in skeletal muscle and enhanced fatty acid-supported respiration, whereas lipid 654 primarily induced transcriptional responses without detectable tissue accumulation. Lipid 1256 increased peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain together with restoration of Parkin, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) while reducing nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) and interleukin 6 (IL-6) expression and preserving skeletal muscle cross-sectional area. These findings suggest that gut microbiome-derived glycine lipids are regulators of skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism, and that tissue retention of bacterial lipids influences mitochondrial oxidative remodelling during metabolic stress.

papers.abstract_en: AIM: This study investigated the emotional responses and underlying psychological processes experienced by nurses in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) following unsuccessful neonatal resuscitation. BACKGROUND: Nurses, particularly neonatal nurses, experience substantial psychological pressure and multifaceted challenges in the aftermath of resuscitation failure. Although existing literature has examined nurses' emotional responses to neonatal death, a significant gap persists in understanding the distinct psychological experiences of neonatal nurses following unsuccessful resuscitation attempts. METHODS: This was a descriptive phenomenological study. Purposive sampling was employed to recruit 14 NICU nurses from a tertiary hospital in Chengdu, Sichuan Province. Participants were selected based on their firsthand experiences of neonatal resuscitation failure and participated in semistructured, face-to-face interviews. The interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-step method. RESULTS: NICU nurses described their personal experiences following failed neonatal resuscitation. Four themes emerged concerning nurses' experiences and growth following resuscitation failure: (1) physical and mental exhaustion; (2) communication challenges; (3) reflection and support needs; and (4) achievements and growth. CONCLUSION: This study revealed the complex psychological experiences of NICU nurses following resuscitation failure. These findings highlight opportunities to support nurses' professional growth and improve team culture and care systems. Consequently, establishing a multidimensional support system is important to support nurses involved in neonatal resuscitation. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING MANAGEMENT: Nurse managers and hospital administrators should establish a comprehensive, multidimensional support system to improve nursing competencies. This system should prioritize standardized training in the theoretical knowledge and practical skills needed for emergency care, while also strengthening nurses' capacity to provide humanistic care.

papers.abstract_en: Targeted therapeutic peptides (TTPs) represent a promising therapeutic modality that bridges the gap between small-molecule drugs and macromolecular antibody-based therapeutics by combining high target specificity, superior tissue permeability, and controllable synthesis. Recent advances in chemical modification and computational design have accelerated the clinical translation of TTPs across diverse therapeutic areas, generating multidimensional data that encompass pharmaceutical profiles, structural binding insights, and structure-activity relationships. However, these data remain fragmented across disparate sources, and no dedicated platform exists to systematically integrate them for mechanistic exploration or rational peptide engineering. Here, we present TTPdb, a specialized database that consolidates comprehensive information on TTPs. TTPdb compiles 5366 TTPs (106 approved, 229 clinical, and 5031 preclinical or investigative), which span >600 disease types and are annotated with 3D structures, binding interactions, and physicochemical properties. TTPdb further catalogs peptide structural modifications and pharmacological mechanisms while establishing associations among peptides, targets, and diseases. TTPdb incorporates a multidimensional search module that supports universal keyword queries, structured conditional filtering, and FASTA-based sequence homology searches, with peptides, targets, and diseases as the primary search entities. As a valuable resource for rational peptide design and optimization in AI-driven biomedical research, TTPdb is freely accessible at https://idrblab.org/TTPdb.

papers.abstract_en: Heme, a redox-active cofactor for vital processes across all domains of life, has widespread applications in healthcare and food supplement industries. However, heme in excess not only inhibits its own synthesis but also is highly cytotoxic, becoming a hindrance for microbial production of heme. In order to pin down heme exporters exploitable for production of secretory heme in bacteria, in this study, we carried out a comprehensive comparative study of heme exporters known to date, CydDC, HrtAB, and CcmABC(D). While CydDC proteins are ubiquitous, homologs of HrtAB and CcmABC(D) are restricted to Gram+ and proteobacteria respectively. We substantiate that CcmB, rather than CcmC or CcmCD, are able to extrude heme out of the membrane, a mechanism shared by HrtB and HrtAB but not CydDC. By expressing CcmB in engineered high-performance heme-producing strains of Escherichia coli, secretory heme production is substantially improved. Our findings offer a solution for high-yield microbial bioproduction of secretory heme with industrial and medical applications.

papers.abstract_en: Effective interaction with complex environments relies on the integration of somatosensory and visual signals into coherent spatial representations of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, as during goal-directed hand movements under mirror-reversed visual feedback, motor performance deteriorates. Despite this conflict, the visual mapping between the hand and the environment remains preserved, and visual information typically facilitates motor performance, whereas tactile feedback impairs it. Here, we tested whether providing tactile input with explicit spatial structure renders visuo-somatosensory integration functionally relevant and stabilizes motor behaviour under sensory conflict. Healthy adults performed a mirror-tracing task, tracing a shape's contour with the index finger while tactile feedback conveyed either motion-related cues alone or additional discrete spatial landmarks aligned with the outline. Spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness relative to motion-related tactile input, indicating more effective online motor control. EEG source analyses further revealed that, when spatial tactile cues were present, somatosensory activity increased and functional connectivity was largely restricted to sensorimotor areas. In contrast, when tactile cues did not convey spatial information, sensory conflict was associated with widespread reductions in cortical activity, including in somatosensory and parietal areas, and with a diffuse functional connectivity pattern consistent with elevated sensorimotor uncertainty. Together, these findings indicate that providing spatial structure to tactile input can mitigate the detrimental effects of visuo-somatosensory conflict on motor performance and support more efficient integration of visual and somatosensory information during action. KEY POINTS: Accurate movements depend on combining visual and somatosensory information to estimate the position of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, motor performance usually deteriorates and tactile feedback can become disruptive. We tested whether tactile feedback becomes useful for movement control when it provides explicit spatial landmarks, rather than only motion-related information from finger-surface contact. During a tracing task under visuo-somatosensory conflict, spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness compared with when touch conveyed motion cues alone. Spatial tactile cues were associated with increased somatosensory cortical activity and a more spatially restricted pattern of functional coupling within sensorimotor networks, whereas their absence was associated with reduced somatosensory and parietal activity and a more distributed connectivity profile. Spatial structure in touch promotes multisensory integration, helping stabilize motor control under sensory conflict and highlighting how tactile cue design may improve sensorimotor function.

papers.authors: Wisdom EM, Goldlist K, Lieber SB, Marwell J, Neukam S, Johnston EA, Batsis JA, Eckstrom E et al.
papers.affiliation_highlight: Medical Scientist Training Program, Oregon Health & Science University, Portland, Oregon, USA.
papers.authors_conclusion: 提出以Geriatrics 5Ms框架（Mind、Mobility、Medications、Multicomplexity、Matters Most）指导老年成人的减重药物处方决策，通过衰弱、认知障碍、糖皮质激素使用与手术规划等老年科常见情景给出兼顾获益与风险的处方路径；认为生活方式共干预，尤其阻抗训练、充足蛋白摄入与持续功能监测，是接受此类治疗老年人的必要组成部分；并提出未来研究优先方向，包括年龄分层临床试验及常规纳入体成分与躯体功能终点。
papers.ai_note: 全文为观点/框架性综述，未提供任何定量数据、系统检索策略或证据分级，属专家建议级别证据；摘要中“相当比例的药物相关减重可能为瘦体重丢失”仅以模糊表述引用“major clinical trials”，未给出具体比例、研究名称或人群，存在以弱证据支撑强警示的倾向；关于围手术期误吸仅作列举，未给出停药间隔或风险量化建议；本文与胸部肿瘤/胸外科业务无直接关联，引用时不可作为GLP-1围手术期管理的量化依据。

papers.abstract_en: Obesity medications that act through gut-derived hormonal pathways include glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1), dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1/GIP), and emerging triple glucagon-like peptide-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon receptor agonists. These therapies are increasingly prescribed for weight management and glycemic control, as well as for their cardiometabolic and renal benefits. While these medications offer substantial benefits to patients across multiple health conditions, their use in older adults warrants heightened scrutiny. Older adults face increased risks of sarcopenia and frailty, and evidence from major clinical trials suggests that a substantial proportion of medication-associated weight loss agents may result in loss of lean mass, potentially posing risks for this population. Other adverse effects that may be more consequential in older adults include dehydration, malnutrition, perioperative aspiration, and fat-predominant weight regain after discontinuation. This paper provides a clinically oriented framework to guide prescribing decisions for older adults. Drawing on patient scenarios from common geriatric contexts, including frailty, cognitive impairment, glucocorticoid use, and surgical planning, we propose prescribing approaches that optimize therapeutic benefits while mitigating potential harms. We integrate these recommendations within the Geriatrics 5Ms Framework (Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most) to contextualize treatment within geriatrics practice. Lifestyle co-interventions, particularly resistance training, adequate protein intake, and ongoing functional monitoring, emerge as essential components for older adults receiving these therapies. We also discuss identifying priority areas for future research, including age-stratified clinical trials and the routine inclusion of body composition and physical function outcomes.

papers.affiliation_highlight: Department of Radiology, Division of Cardiovascular Imaging, Mayo Clinic, 200 1st St SW, Rochester, MN 55905.

papers.abstract_en: Vascular abnormalities are less common in the hand and wrist than in the lower extremities but can result in significant morbidity if unrecognized or untreated. The unique vascular architecture of the hand and wrist, with a dense network of arterial anastomoses, confers resilience to ischemia, but the superficial location makes them vulnerable to trauma and occupational injury. The authors describe and illustrate a comprehensive multimodality imaging approach to the diagnosis and evaluation of vascular abnormalities of the hand and wrist. They begin with an overview of vascular anatomy and normal variants, including a persistent median artery. Multimodality imaging, including US, CT angiography, MR angiography, and digital subtraction angiography, is reviewed with a focus on strengths, limitations, and clinical utility. Dynamic imaging techniques and photon-counting CT are highlighted for their evolving roles. A wide spectrum of vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, trauma, iatrogenic injury, embolism, hypothenar hammer syndrome, hand-arm vibration syndrome, vasculitis, and frostbite, as well as their imaging appearances, are discussed. Vascular anomalies, including vascular malformations and vascular neoplasms, are also reviewed. The role of imaging in hand transplantation is addressed. The authors provide a framework for recognizing vascular diseases in the hand and wrist and selecting the appropriate imaging modality. Familiarity with vascular anatomy, imaging findings, and clinical context is essential for timely diagnosis, guiding management, and preserving limb function.

papers.abstract_en: Addressing the global food shortage crisis requires precise and timely diagnostics of plant exogenous stresses (such as pesticides) to enhance the quality and yield of crops. Plant-wearable sensors (PWS) offer a promising approach to real-time monitoring of pesticides for plant health but remain limited by challenges in low signal-conversion efficiency and poor mechanical adaptability at the plant-sensor interface. Here we report a robust PWS by embedding an aggregation-induced emission (AIE) silver nanoclusters@zeolitic imidazolate framework@polydopamine (AgNCs@ZIF@PDA) composite into a plant-adaptive hydrogel patch, enabling the on-site monitoring of pesticide information. The conformal hydrogel interface of the PWS utilizes an in-situ radical triggered sol-gel phase transition to lock into the abrupt hairy surface irregularities, resolving the issue of mechanical adaptability. The resultant AgNCs@ZIF@PDA-based hydrogel patch exhibits high sensitivity toward 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, with a limit of detection as low as 26.7 ng/mL. Mechanism investigations elucidate that the synergistic combination of the AIE effect of AgNCs and the specific responsive behavior of the heterogeneous interface of PDA enhances the energy-transfer (signal-conversion) efficiency. Notably, the PWS enables non-invasive, continuous quantification of pesticide degradation kinetics. This robust fluorescence PWS enables real-time tracking of pesticides for plant health, thereby advancing the goals of precision chemical application and resource-efficient agriculture.

papers.abstract_en: European Union (EU) authorisation for the gene therapy medicinal product Waskyra® (etuvetidigene autotemcel; hereafter etu-cel) marks a milestone for patients living with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS). The successful regulatory application for Waskyra by a non-profit organisation reflects not only the convincing scientific evidence supporting the authorisation, but also highlights that regulatory support is available from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) to help (small) developers manoeuvre the complexities of gene therapy medicinal product development for rare diseases. Here, we summarise the assessment by the EMA's Committees and present the key aspects underlying the positive outcome. Developers of innovative therapies addressing clear unmet medical needs are encouraged to seek early interaction with the EMA to help them design robust development programs and access supportive pathways that facilitate and accelerate development and evaluation.

papers.abstract_en: The capacity to regulate corticosterone release following a stressful event is an essential component of the physiological flexibility required to maintain homeostasis and ensure adaptive responses to environmental change. We show that wild smooth-fronted caimans with elevated blood mercury (Hg) concentrations exhibited reduced peak corticosterone levels during standardized stress tests, indicating a dampened maximal stress response. Hg blood concentrations were negatively correlated with corticosterone responsiveness, suggesting impairment of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function. These results demonstrate that environmental Hg contamination is associated with reduced stress responsiveness and physiological flexibility, which likely limits the ability of Hg-contaminated individuals to cope with novel environmental stressors. We found that a methylmercury-sensitive cysteine in the glucocorticoid receptor is highly conserved across vertebrates, suggesting a shared molecular mechanism for mercury effects on glucocorticoid signaling. Given the widespread Hg pollution in tropical ecosystems, these findings emphasize the role of Hg as an endocrine-disrupting chemical in crocodylians.

papers.abstract_en: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global public health challenge, with treatment complicated by drug resistance, adverse effects, and suboptimal host immune responses. Whilst conventional anti-TB drugs are effective bactericidally, their immunomodulatory effects may, in certain contexts, contribute to immune imbalance and affect treatment outcomes. Host-directed therapy (HDT), which aims to modulate the host immune response to enhance pathogen control and limit immunopathology, has emerged as a promising adjunctive strategy. This narrative review critically evaluates the current evidence for HDT in TB, focusing on immunosenescence, trained immunity, cytokine and lipid mediator networks, immunometabolic reprogramming, neuroendocrine regulation, and repurposed drugs including metformin and statins. Importantly, we distinguish between evidence derived directly from TB models (in vitro, animal, and clinical studies) and evidence extrapolated from other diseases, highlighting knowledge gaps and areas requiring further investigation. We propose that future progress depends on evidence-based stratification of HDT candidates, rigorous clinical trial design, and a personalised approach that accounts for patient comorbidities and immune status. This review aims to provide a balanced framework for advancing HDT from bench to bedside in TB therapy.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Mass casualty incidents (MCI) are of significant public health concern. Most health facilities in developing countries often struggle to be fully prepared for MCI. MCI preparedness among other factors involves important processes like communication among staff on the emergency response team, patients, and the public; and the coordination of emergency care services delivery. In this study, we explored staff experiences at a district-level university hospital in Ghana regarding communication and coordination during MCI. METHODS: We conducted an exploratory descriptive qualitative study at a University Hospital between August 2024 and February 2025. We collected data through in-depth interviews. We used a purposive sample of 15 hospital staff. The interview sessions were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. We analyzed the data using Braun and Clarke's (2006) thematic analysis and reflexive thematic analysis approach (2021). RESULTS: A total of 15 participants (doctors, nurses, pharmacists, medical laboratory scientist, and administrative staff) were interviewed. Thematic analysis of the data revealed two major themes (communication and coordination) and six sub-themes. The communication sub-theme encompassed internal and external communication as well as communication challenges. The coordination sub-theme comprised decision-making and leadership structures, human resource mobilization, and teamwork and support roles. Internal communication was mostly done through hospital landlines and mobile phones whereas external communication was achieved through Mutual Aid Agreements with other hospitals. Communication challenges included being unable to reach other wards on the landlines and the feedback received about the unavailability of beds at the external facilities. There was no clear leadership structure, leading to ad hoc decision-making by the senior-most medical officer on duty. However, teamwork within the emergency unit was effective during MCIs management. Human resource mobilization was done through staff redeployments from other wards to the emergency unit during patient surge. CONCLUSIONS: Despite good teamwork and fast mobilization of human resources during MCI, the findings of this study identified gaps in communication networks and absence of designated leadership structures. Implementing standardized communication protocols, clearly defined leadership structures, and improving coordination mechanisms between hospitals may enhance emergency care delivery during MCIs.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Middle-aged women face distinct physiological, psychological, and social challenges during the transition from adulthood to later life. However, their perceptions of aging and the strategies they employ to cope with this process remain insufficiently understood. This qualitative study aimed to explore how middle-aged women perceive and respond to aging, with the goal of informing the development of future assessment instruments and targeted health interventions. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 middle-aged women aged 46-57 years in Changsha, Hunan Province, from April to June 2025. Participants represented diverse educational backgrounds, residential areas, and menopausal statuses. Thematic analysis was employed for data analysis, and the study adhered to the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist. RESULTS: The perceptions and coping strategies of middle-aged women regarding aging were categorized into five themes, summarized as "1H4W": (1) H- "How am I aging": A three-dimensional experience of aging; (2) W1- "What does aging bring me": The dual impact of aging; (3) W2- "Why am I aging": Multidimensional attribution of aging; (4) W3- "What can I do": Dual trajectories of coping strategies and their perceived efficacy; (5) W4- "What prevents me from acting": Barriers to aging coping actions. CONCLUSIONS: Middle-aged women experience complex and multifaceted perceptions of aging, encompassing physical, psychological, and social dimensions. Their perceptions reflect both threat and growth, and their attribution patterns influence their choices of coping behaviors. However, translating these perceptions into action faces significant barriers. These preliminary findings point toward the potential value of developing a validated tool to assess aging perceptions in middle-aged women, which may enhance self-awareness, promote proactive health behaviors, and support healthy aging.

papers.abstract_en: Changes in adipose tissue function, morphology, and secretome during obesity impair endothelial cell function and lead to persistent hypoxia and unresolved inflammation, which will contribute to whole-body endothelial dysfunction and chronic low-grade inflammation. Indeed, visceral fat dysfunction is more associated with insulin resistance than body mass index. Understanding the molecular landscape of visceral adipose tissue is pivotal to better comprehending an individual's metabolic health and even predicting future health outcomes. Single-cell studies are showing that the heterogeneity of the adipose depots relies not only on the diversity of cellular types, but also on the differential gene expression and secretome (even within the same cellular type). Adipose tissue cells respond in an orchestrated manner to adequate tissue plasticity to the current energetic needs, either by expanding or retracting. This response relies on coordinated regulation of adipocyte metabolism, angiogenesis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and short-term inflammation and oxidative stress. In this review, we look closely at cell intercommunication in the fat depot and discuss the main events occurring in adipose tissue associated with the progressive tissue dysfunction that happens in obesity: adipocyte metabolism, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Furthermore, we discuss the modulation of angiogenesis as a potential therapeutic target in obesity by gathering relevant recent research and collectively discuss the metabolic implications of inhibiting or promoting angiogenesis at different stages of the metabolic sequelae of obesity.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Metabolic reprogramming of tumor cells interacts with functional alterations of immune cells to establish an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which constrains the efficacy of immunotherapy. Nanomedicine provides technical approaches for targeted delivery and controlled release of metabolic modulators. MAIN TEXT: This review outlines major nanocarriers and their design principles, dissects the crosstalk among glucose, amino acid and lipid metabolism, and illustrates how nutrient competition and metabolic byproducts shape antitumor immune responses. It focuses on summarizing advances in nanodelivery strategies targeting these metabolic pathways and their combinatorial application with immunotherapy. CONCLUSION: Nanomedicine-mediated metabolic intervention holds promise for remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment. However, tumor cells and effector T cells share partial metabolic requirements, and nonselective inhibition may impair antitumor immunity. Improving the cell selectivity of interventions and validating long-term safety and clinical benefits represent key considerations for future translational research.

papers.abstract_en: The Siglec-sialoglycan axis is an emerging glyco-immune checkpoint in cancer. This is supported by the frequent upregulation of both Siglecs and sialoglycans in the tumor microenvironment. Siglecs are receptors expressed on immune cells that recognize sialoglycans, carbohydrate structures terminated by sialic acid. Most Siglec receptor family members are inhibitory and suppress immune cell activation through the recruitment of SHP-1 and SHP-2 phosphatases. It is well established that Siglecs expressed by immune cells bind ligands present on other cells, including tumor and stromal cells (trans-interactions). However, immune cells themselves also express sialoglycans that can serve as ligands for Siglecs on the same cell surface (cis-interactions). Over the past two decades, numerous studies have addressed how Siglec trans-engagement facilitates immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment. The role of cis-interactions in regulating Siglec function and their impact on immune cell activity, however, remains an underexplored topic for most Siglec family members. This review discusses how cis-ligands modulate Siglec function, the mechanisms regulating sialic acid expression on immune cell surfaces, and the functional relevance of cis-interactions expressed by immune cells in the tumor microenvironment. A better understanding of these processes may facilitate the development of next-generation therapeutics targeting the Siglec-sialoglycan axis in cancer.

papers.abstract_en: The human gut microbiota is a vast and intricate microbial ecosystem that plays indispensable roles in host physiology, including nutritional metabolism, immune system development, and disease prevention. While current research has extensively focused on microbiota-derived small-molecule metabolites and virulence-associated factors, the functional contribution of gut bacteria-derived proteins remains comparatively underexplored. These proteins are emerging as key molecular mediators of host-microbe and microbe-microbe interactions. In this review, we synthesize current evidence to delineate the potential links between the spatial distribution, sources and ecological niches of gut microbiota and the repertoire of proteins they produce. We systematically categorize the functions and mechanisms of diverse bacterial-derived beneficial proteins, including enzymes, surface-associated proteins, outer membrane vesicle-associated proteins, and secreted effectors, highlighting their critical roles in antimicrobial defense, metabolic homeostasis, immune modulation, and antitumor activity from multiple perspectives. Particular emphasis is also placed on their distinct molecular strategies in mediating host interactions. Collectively, this analysis underscores the translational potential of gut microbiota-derived proteins, pointing toward innovative applications in the rational design of next-generation postbiotics, engineered bacterial proteins, and potential microbiome-based biologic therapeutics.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Rheumatoid arthritis remains a leading cause of irreversible joint disability worldwide. Triptolide and celastrol, major bioactive compounds derived from Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F. (TwHF), have substantial therapeutic potential for rheumatoid arthritis. However, poor solubility, low oral bioavailability, narrow therapeutic windows, and dose-limiting systemic toxicity limit their clinical translation. OBJECTIVE: This review integrates the anti-rheumatoid arthritis mechanisms of triptolide and celastrol with recent advances in nanodelivery systems to establish a mechanism-guided framework for nanocarrier design and clinical translation. RESULTS: Triptolide and celastrol exert multifaceted anti-rheumatoid arthritis effects by inhibiting inflammatory signaling pathways, regulating macrophage polarization and T-cell homeostasis, suppressing fibroblast-like synoviocyte proliferation, and protecting bone and cartilage. Diverse nanodelivery platforms-including lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, biomimetic, carrier-free, and hybrid systems-have substantially improved the bioavailability and lesion-targeting capability of triptolide and celastrol, achieving superior anti-inflammatory and joint-protective efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity. CONCLUSION: Mechanism-guided nanodelivery may help translate triptolide and celastrol into safer, targeted rheumatoid arthritis therapies. Realizing this potential requires a shift from material-centric research toward application-oriented development supported by rigorous validation.

papers.abstract_en: Sugar crops including sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum, are fundamental for global sucrose supply and crucial feedstocks for bioethanol production and industrial bioproducts. However, yield and sucrose accumulation are significantly influenced by abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity/alkalinity, heat, chilling/freezing, and heavy metal toxicity. The polygenic complexity of stress tolerance, particularly in sugarcane with its large, polyploid, and haplotype-diverse genome, presents significant challenges for conventional breeding, rendering it slow and imprecise. This review combines advances in genome-editing technologies, including CRISPR/Cas systems (Cas9 and Cas12a), along with transcriptional techniques (CRISPRa/i), base editors, and prime editors. These tools, combined with the progress in reference genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and pangenomes, have facilitated precise gene discovery, genomic selection, and targeted editing. CRISPR-based approaches offer promising avenues for enhancing key stress-responsive pathways governing oxidative homeostasis, membrane integrity, osmotic regulation, hormone signaling, and ion-homeostasis in sugar crops. Prominent candidate targets include transcription factors (TF), signaling components, raffinose biosynthesis genes implicated in freezing tolerance, regulators of salt and alkaline stress, and determinants of heavy metal tolerance and sequestration. Translational challenges, such as off-target effects, low transformation efficiencies, and editing multiple homologues or haplotypes, are being addressed such as DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, high-throughput screening, haplotype-specific target design, and haplotype-aware guide RNA engineering based on unique genetic variation sites across different gene haplotypes. Collectively, the integration of advanced CRISPR toolkits with enhanced genomic information resources and phenotyping capabilities holds significant potential for accelerating the development of precision-bred, multi-stress-resilient sugar crops that sustain yield, quality, and industrial value under abiotic stress conditions.

papers.abstract_en: RATIONALE: Self-directed lifestyle interventions may improve access to weight loss care in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but effectiveness in routine practice is unknown. OBJECTIVE: Test whether a proactively delivered self-directed lifestyle intervention improves weight and sleep-related quality of life versus usual care. METHODS: POWER enrolled patients with OSA and body mass index of 30-45 kg/m2, recruited from Veteran Affairs (VA) sites nationwide, and randomized participants to a self-directed intervention based on the Diabetes Prevention Program with video-based sessions, readings, and regular coaching reminders or usual care. Co-primary outcomes were change in Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire (FOSQ) and clinical weight in kilograms (kg) from baseline to 12 months post-randomization. Given two primary outcomes, we defined significance at p = 0.025. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: This trial randomized 696 participants. Mean age was 56.2 years (SD 12.2), with 19.7% identifying as female. Clinical weights at 12 months were available for 81.9% of intervention and 83.6% of control participants. Unadjusted weight declined 2.1 kg (SD 6.8) in intervention and 0.9 kg (SD 5.9) in control (adjusted between-group difference: -1.1 kg, 95%CI -2.0, -0.1; p = 0.037). FOSQ measures were available at 12 months for 78.2% of intervention and 90.5% of control participants. From baseline to 12 months, unadjusted FOSQ improved 1.4 (SD 2.7) points in intervention and 0.9 (SD 2.9) points in control (adjusted between-group difference: 0.6 points, 95%CI 0.2, 1.0; p = 0.001). CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: Among participants with OSA and obesity, a self-directed lifestyle intervention did not improve weight loss and led to improvements in sleep-related quality of life that are of limited clinical importance. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05104450, registered 10/19/2021.

papers.abstract_en: RATIONALE: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the accepted first-line treatment for insomnia, but its scalability and safety in patients with co-morbid insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea (COMISA) remain unclear. Clinician-guided digital CBT-I (D-CBT-I) is a potential treatment option that may address these limitations in COMISA. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician-guided D-CBT-I versus sleep hygiene education (SHE) in patients with COMISA. METHODS: This randomized trial (n = 88) compared clinician-guided D-CBT-I (6 weekly online sessions: sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention) with SHE alone. Blinded outcome assessments were conducted at baseline, posttreatment (6 weeks), and 3-month follow-up. Primary outcomes were Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores at posttreatment and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included daytime sleepiness, sleep parameters, OSA severity, neurocognitive function, and adverse events. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: At 3-month follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis showed significantly greater improvements with D-CBT-I versus SHE on ISI (-9.5 vs. -4.0 points; d = -1.18, P = 0.001) and PSQI (-4.9 vs. -1.8 points; d = -0.87, P = 0.001); D-CBT-I also reduced subjective sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale; -3.4 vs. -1.0 points; d = -0.68, P < 0.001). At posttreatment, D-CBT-I reduced the apnea-hypopnea index (attended in-laboratory polysomnography; -6.0 vs. +2.0 events/h; d = -0.64, P = 0.019). Although transient increases in ESS occurred at weeks 2-4, no functional impairment or sleepiness-related adverse events were reported. Additional benefits were observed in metacognition and executive function. CONCLUSION: Clinician-guided D-CBT-I improved insomnia and OSA severity, and enhanced cognitive function in COMISA patients. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry; NO.: ChiCTR2500099854; URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=267457.

papers.abstract_en: The clinical adoption of deep learning in pathology is largely hindered by the "black box" nature of current models, which often obscure the biological basis of prognosis. Here, we introduce MorphX, an interpretable framework that predicts patient survival by explicitly decoding multi-scale morphological patterns from whole-slide images. Unlike conventional methods relying on latent features, MorphX fuses macro-scale tissue texture with micro-scale nuclear metrics to attribute risk to interpretable biological phenotypes. In a multi-center study spanning 1,067 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), MorphX achieves concordance indices of 0.775-0.799 in discovery cohorts. Crucially, we derive eight distinct morphology-based biomarkers-driven by texture heterogeneity in necrotic regions, lymphocyte density, and nuclear shape-that demonstrate reproducible survival associations across independent cohorts, offering a granular resolution of tumor aggressiveness that transcends traditional histological grading. By translating opaque computational predictions into validated biological insights, MorphX supports trustworthy, transparent, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven precision oncology.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA. RESULTS: A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84-1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ. CONCLUSIONS: In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Regisrty- India (CTRI) identifier [CTRI/2024/02/062201], registered [01 February 2024].

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Small-for-gestational age birth and infant linear growth faltering are prevalent in South Asia. The World Health Organization recommends balanced energy-protein (BEP) supplementation in pregnancy for undernourished populations, but evidence on the extension of supplementation through lactation to improve infant growth remains limited. OBJECTIVE: To examine the effect of daily fortified BEP supplementation during pregnancy and lactation on infant mean length-for-age z-score (LAZ) and secondary growth outcomes at 6 months of age. METHODS: MINT (Maternal Infant Nutrition Trial) was a 2x2 factorial, household randomized, unblinded efficacy trial to assess a daily fortified BEP supplement during pregnancy and/or lactation compared to no supplement on birth and infant growth outcomes in Sarlahi, Nepal. A modified intention-to-treat analysis estimated the effects of supplementation on infant growth outcomes using linear and Poisson regression models. Models without and with adjustment for birth size were used to estimate the overall effect and the effect independent of birth size, respectively. RESULTS: Among 1,554 mothers and 1,568 infants randomized after delivery, there was no interaction between pregnancy and lactation supplementation on the primary infant growth outcome. Neither BEP supplementation during pregnancy nor lactation had an effect on mean infant LAZ at 6 months (unadjusted mean difference for pregnancy: 0.01 [95% CI: -0.10, 0.12]; for lactation -0.02 [95% CI: -0.13, 0.09]). Significant differences were not observed for any secondary outcomes: mean weight-for-length z-scores, weight-for-age z-scores, infant weight, length, head circumference, mid-upper arm circumference or prevalence of stunting, wasting, and underweight at 6-months or for a subset of infants at 12-months. Null effects persisted after adjustment for birth size. CONCLUSIONS: In rural Nepal, daily fortified BEP supplementation during pregnancy or early lactation did not improve linear or ponderal growth of infants at 6- or 12-months. To reduce the burden of early infant growth faltering, alternative strategies should be considered. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT03668977. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03668977?term=nct03668977&rank=1.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Depemokimab is the first ultra-long-acting biologic, with enhanced interleukin-5 binding affinity, high potency, and extended half-life, enabling twice-yearly dosing. The double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3a SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 studies demonstrated depemokimab efficacy and safety over 52 weeks in patients with asthma with type 2 inflammation and an eosinophilic phenotype. Here, we present long-term safety and efficacy outcomes over the 52-week, phase 3a open-label extension (OLE) of SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 (AGILE) alongside an integrated post-hoc analysis of the 104-week SWIFT and AGILE period. METHODS: In SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2, patients (aged ≥12 years) with asthma with type 2 inflammation, an eosinophilic phenotype (≥150 cells/μL at screening or ≥300 cells/μL during the previous 12 months), and a history of at least two exacerbations in the previous 12 months despite receiving medium-dose or high-dose inhaled corticosteroids were randomly assigned (2:1) to subcutaneous depemokimab 100 mg or placebo every 26 weeks in addition to standard of care for 52 weeks. Patients who completed SWIFT-1 or SWIFT-2 could join the single-arm, 52-week AGILE OLE study, conducted at 156 centres across 14 countries. Patients continued depemokimab (depemokimab-depemokimab group) or switched to depemokimab from placebo (placebo-depemokimab group). The primary endpoints for the 52-week AGILE OLE period were the incidence of adverse events and serious adverse events, and immunogenicity as measured by the presence of anti-drug antibodies and neutralising antibodies. Secondary efficacy outcomes, including exacerbation rate, St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) total score, Asthma Control Questionnaire-5 (ACQ-5) score, and pre-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1), were also assessed. Additional post-hoc analyses were carried out to assess safety and efficacy over the 104-week integrated SWIFT and AGILE analysis period. AGILE OLE is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05243680. The SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04719832 and NCT04718103. FINDINGS: Between March 1, 2022, and May 19, 2025, 629 patients were included in the AGILE OLE study (419 patients in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 210 patients in the placebo-depemokimab group). During the 52-week AGILE OLE period, adverse events occurred in 297 (71%) of 419 patients in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 146 (70%) of 210 patients in the placebo-depemokimab group; serious adverse events were infrequent (37 [9%] of 419 in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 19 [9%] of 210 in the placebo-depemokimab group), with no treatment-related or fatal serious adverse events reported. In the depemokimab-depemokimab group, the reduced annualised exacerbation rate was sustained over 2 years (0·51 [95% CI 0·43-0·61] in the 52-week SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 period and 0·56 [0·47-0·66] in the AGILE OLE). Improvements in SGRQ total score, ACQ-5 score, and FEV1 were maintained over 2 years. In the placebo-depemokimab group, improvements in clinical outcomes were observed after the switch to depemokimab during the AGILE OLE. INTERPRETATION: Twice-yearly depemokimab was well tolerated and demonstrated sustained efficacy over the 2-year SWIFT and AGILE period, supporting its long-term therapeutic benefit and safety profile. papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: The advent of regulatory-approved pharmacological treatments for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) calls for precise, non-invasive biomarkers that facilitate early diagnosis, support therapy selection, and aid clinical trial enrolment. The European multicentre LITMUS study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of a broad range of non-invasive biomarkers for identifying patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), at-risk MASH, advanced fibrosis, and cirrhosis. METHODS: In this prospective, multicentre, diagnostic accuracy study, adults with biopsy-confirmed MASLD were prospectively recruited across 13 countries in Europe and the USA. We assessed 12 single markers and 18 multimarker panels. The reference standard was centrally scored liver histology according to the non-alcoholic steatohepatitis Clinical Research Network Scoring System. Target conditions included MASH (Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease Activity Score ≥4 with ≥1 point per component), at-risk MASH (MASH plus significant fibrosis [fibrosis stage F≥2]), advanced fibrosis (F≥3), and cirrhosis (F4). Performance was evaluated by area-under-the-receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with the minimum acceptable criterion (MAC) of AUC higher than 0·80 to indicate potential biopsy replacement. FINDINGS: Between Jan 1, 2018, and June 30, 2023, we analysed data from 1590 participants with centrally scored liver biopsies and at least one biomarker measurement; 609 (38%) had biopsy-confirmed at-risk MASH, 678 (43%) had MASH, 585 (37%) had advanced fibrosis, and 164 (10%) had cirrhosis. For detecting at-risk MASH, SomaSignal showed the highest diagnostic performance (AUC 0·83 [95% CI 0·80-0·85]), significantly exceeding MAC, whereas no other test reached the MAC for MASH only. For advanced fibrosis, SomaSignal showed the highest performance (AUC 0·92 [0·90-0·94]), followed by FibroMeter-VCTE (AUC 0·87 [0·83-0·92]), Agile 3+ and TSP2 (both AUC 0·84 [0·82-0·86]), and NIS4 (0·82 [0·80-0·85]). For cirrhosis, FibroMeter-VCTE showed the highest diagnostic performance (AUC 0·94 [0·90-0·97]) followed by SomaSignal (AUC 0·92 [0·90-0·94]), followed by Agile 3+ (0·88 [0·85-0·91]), Agile 4 (0·87 [0·84-0·90]), ADAPT (0·85 [0·81-0·88]), and ELF, LSM-VCTE, and TSP2 (all 0·84 [0·81-0·87]). Sequential two-step approaches using gamma-glutamyl transferase as a first-line test met the MAC for both advanced fibrosis and at-risk MASH. INTERPRETATION: Although single markers resulted in variable and limited performance when compared to histology for detecting at-risk MASH, multimarker panels showed great potential, with a proteomic panel showing strong diagnostic performance. These findings could support the selection and implementation of non-invasive testing strategies in MASLD and inform future clinical guidelines, regulatory evaluation, and clinical trial design. FUNDING: Innovative Medicines Initiative 2 Joint Undertaking.

We conducted a retrospective, single-center cohort study of adults with group 1 PAH. Patients prescribed SGLT2i were compared with patients without exposure. Propensity-score matching was performed 1:2 using age, sex, baseline REVEAL Lite 2 risk category, diabetes mellitus, and statin use. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events. Associations were evaluated using fixed-exposure and start-stop time-varying Cox models. The matched cohort included 366 patients: 122 (33%) receiving SGLT2i and 244 (67%) controls. Most patients were classified as high risk by REVEAL Lite 2 (106 SGLT2i recipients (87%) and 215 controls (88%), respectively). In the fixed-exposure analysis, SGLT2i use was associated with lower mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 0.53; 95% CI, 0.31-0.91; P=.018), without a significant difference in major adverse cardiovascular events (HR, 1.23; 95% CI, 0.93-1.63; P=.14). In the time-varying analysis, SGLT2i exposure was not significantly associated with mortality (HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.26-2.11; P=.57). The apparent survival association was attenuated after accounting for treatment timing, demonstrating the sensitivity of observational PAH estimates to exposure classification and supporting prospective randomized trials.

papers.abstract_en: UNLABELLED: Phototherapies play an important role in the treatment of hyperpigmentation. However, the effects of different phototherapies on skin pigmentation have not been comprehensively evaluated to date. We analyzed the efficacy and patient satisfaction of 14 distinct phototherapies for melasma using a network meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials. Cluster analysis revealed that fractional CO2 laser combines the advantages of high efficacy and patient satisfaction. We therefore evaluated the effect of fractional CO2 laser on forearm skin pigmentation in volunteers. Reflectance confocal microscopy showed that fractional CO2 laser effectively inhibited pigmentation, and the inhibitory effect was more pronounced as the scanning spacing decreased. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis revealed that fractional CO2 laser inhibited melanogenesis in photoaging skin. Transcriptome sequencing of skin samples from guinea pigs treated with fractional CO2 laser showed that the key regulators of melanogenesis (microphthalmia-associated transcription factor, tyrosinase and dopachrome tautomerase) were significantly downregulated on the seventh day after treatment with fractional CO2 laser. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis further revealed that the cyclic adenosine monophosphate signaling pathway was inhibited on the third day after treatment, whereas the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-protein kinase B pathway was activated on the fifth and seventh days. Fractional CO2 laser effectively reversed hyperpigmentation and may even inhibit skin pigmentation by exfoliating the superficial stratum corneum, destroying melanin granules, and regulating signaling pathways related to melanogenesis. papers.abstract_en: Lung cancer associated with cystic airspaces (LCCA) is an increasingly recognised yet under-characterised presentation of non-small cell lung cancer, accounting for approximately 1-4% of cases. Despite growing awareness driven by thin-section computed tomography and lung cancer screening, LCCA remains absent from major international guidelines and classifications, including those of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer, and the World Health Organization. This narrative review synthesises the available evidence to define LCCA as a distinct clinico-radiological entity and to inform future guideline development. LCCA presents heterogeneously, with thin- or thick walled cysts, unilocular or multiloculated morphology, and variable solid components, frequently mimicking benign cysts, bullae, or emphysema. Such ambiguity contributes to diagnostic delay; in the NELSON screening trial, LCCA accounted for 22.7% of missed or delayed diagnoses. Several radiological classifications, notably that of Mascalchi, aid description and risk stratification. Conventional staging is problematic, as measurement of the solid component alone may underestimate true tumour extent, while fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography carries a high false-negative rate. Tissue sampling is similarly complicated by low diagnostic yield and false negative results, underscoring the importance of multidisciplinary team discussion. The natural history follows a stepwise progression from thin-walled cyst to wall thickening, mural nodularity, and invasive disease, with prognosis determined principally by stage, although mural nodularity and increasing solid components confer higher recurrence risk. Treatment broadly mirrors that of solid lung tumours; current guidance advocates targeting the whole cystic lesion for radical therapy rather than the solid component alone, with systemic anticancer therapy appropriate in advanced or multifocal disease. Much current practice is extrapolated from part-solid tumours; consensus on Powered by Editorial Manager® and ProduXion Manager® from Aries Systems Corporation terminology, classification, and staging, supported by prospective registry data, is required to optimise outcomes.

papers.abstract_en: Rapid pathogen identification is critical for timely antibiotic therapy in patients with pneumonia, yet current methods remain too slow or complex for routine clinical use. Here, we describe a localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR)-based biosensor platform that detects Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria directly in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) without nucleic acid extraction or amplification. Gold nano-islands (AuNIs) functionalized with antibodies against lipoteichoic acid (LTA) or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) enabled selective bacterial capture. The sensor achieved a refractive index resolution of 8.52 × 10-8 RIU with good reusability and dynamic range. Detection limits reached the concentration of 0.027 μM for purified LTA and 0.208 endotoxin units (EU) for LPS. When tested with Escherichia coli in artificial samples, the LPS sensor showed a reproducibility standard deviation (RSD) of 3.14%, detecting bacterial growth significantly earlier than conventional OD600 measurement. In 33 clinical BALF samples, sensor results correlated strongly with standard diagnostics (Pearson r = 0.963) and distinguished infected from noninfected cases using cutoff values of 0.060 rad (Gram-positive) and 0.083 rad (Gram-negative). The platform detects polymyxin B susceptibility 8 h earlier than conventional OD600 measurements, and a proof-of-concept sandwich immunoassay enables species-level discrimination between E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. With excellent reproducibility (RSD = 3.14%), reusability over six cycles (84.21% ± 2.03% signal retention), and four-week storage stability (98.63% ± 5.42%), this LSPR platform offers a practical, rapid approach for frontline bacterial screening and accelerated antibiotic stewardship in pneumonia.

papers.abstract_en: Irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhoea are disorders of gut-brain interaction, the symptoms of which include abnormal stool consistency or frequency accompanied by varying degrees of abdominal pain, discomfort, bloating, or distension. These conditions affect 20% of the global population with a relapsing and remitting course. Risk factors include female sex, younger age, a history of common mental disorders, and acute enteric infection. The pathophysiology of irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhoea remain incompletely understood, but are thought to be secondary to aberrant interactions throughout the gut-brain axis, resulting in disordered gut motility and visceral hypersensitivity. These conditions are diagnosed with a combination of clinical history, absence of alarm symptoms-such as weight loss or rectal bleeding-and targeted investigations. An empathetic management approach improves quality of life and symptoms, reduces health-care use, and enhances treatment adherence. Mainstays of treatment include education, dietary and lifestyle advice, modifying fibre intake, and drugs directed towards predominant symptoms. For severe symptoms, other treatments include specific medical devices, biofeedback, or psychological therapies. However, the effectiveness of most treatments is modest and there is an ongoing need to expand available treatments for bowel disorders, with several novel drugs currently in development.

papers.abstract_en: Males have lower life expectancies and greater disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) than females, and particularly poor outcomes are seen among males in marginalised contexts. In this paper, we provide an epidemiological overview and highlight the intersectional nature of men's health. We analyse mortality and DALYs data from the 1990-2023 Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Studies to illustrate our intersectional framework and draw attention to how health varies in men and to show key themes. Conditions that contribute most to the poor health of males include non-communicable diseases (eg, cardiovascular diseases and cancers), substance use, suicide, injuries (eg, road traffic incidents and interpersonal violence), and respiratory infections (eg, tuberculosis and COVID-19). Although cardiovascular disease and cancer make the largest contributions to men's higher mortality rates, determinants of health such as violence and war, migration, economic stagnation, and labour market changes due to automation and new technologies will disproportionally affect their health in the future. Injuries, violence, and other external morbidity causes often occur at a young age and in unequal distributions across the sexes, making a large contribution to DALYs. Although biology plays a role, the pattern of many diseases contributing to health differences reflects the intersection of health behaviours, shaped by patriarchy, ideas of masculinity, and structural drivers (including commercial determinants of health); many of these are preventable. Although improvements in some health behaviours are seen, exceptions occur in marginalising social conditions (eg, incarcerated men, men experiencing homelessness, men with mental illnesses, men with substance use disorders, men with low income, men who have sex with men, and those who are gender non-conforming). Multiple data sources detail men's shorter life expectancies and the drivers compared with women, but going beyond sex disaggregation remains challenging and is an urgent priority for research and health monitoring.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: The 2024 McDonald criteria broaden the definition of multiple sclerosis (MS), enabling diagnosis in individuals with asymptomatic MRI findings or clinical presentations not meeting the 2017 criteria. We assessed whether these criteria identify such cases using independent laboratory/imaging biomarkers and whether these biomarkers predict subsequent disease activity. METHODS: Participants with asymptomatic MRI findings or clinical presentations not meeting the 2017 criteria were included and stratified according to the 2024 criteria. Serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL) and 3T brain MRI measures-including normalised brain volumes, T2 lesion load (T2LL), cortical lesion (CL) and paramagnetic rim lesion (PRL)-were compared between McDonald2024-positive and McDonald2024-negative groups, and with age/sex matched McDonald2017-positive cases according to the 2017 criteria; predictors of disease activity were assessed using penalised-Cox regression. FINDINGS: A total of 141 participants were included: 95 not meeting the 2017 criteria (n = 64 asymptomatic MRI findings; n = 31 clinical presentations), stratified as McDonald2024-positive (n = 46) or McDonald2024-negative (n = 49), and 46 McDonald2017-positive cases. McDonald2024-positive vs. McDonald2024-negative cases showed higher age-corrected sNfL Z-scores (median 0.28[IQR 0.76] vs. -0.12[0.82], p = 0.003/pFDR = 0.006), reduced normalised thalamic volume (mean 0.009±[SD]0.0007 vs. 0.010 ± 0.0007, p = 0.003/pFDR = 0.006), and higher CL (1[4] vs. 0[0], p < 0.001/pFDR < 0.001) and PRL (1[1] vs. 0[0], p < 0.001/pFDR = 0.003) counts (differences remaining significant after age/sex, disease duration and T2LL adjustments). Biomarker profiles were comparable between McDonald2024-positive and McDonald2017-positive cases. Penalised-Cox regression (n = 52) identified sNfL Z-score and PRL presence as the most consistently selected predictors of disease activity, with higher bootstrap stability for sNfL (0.84) than PRL (0.76), and good model discrimination (C-index = 0.71). INTERPRETATION: The 2024 McDonald criteria identify individuals not meeting the 2017 criteria who already exhibit MS-like neuroinflammatory/neurodegenerative pathological changes. These are reflected by laboratory and imaging biomarkers, including sNfL, which may predict subsequent disease activity and complement current diagnostic frameworks to support early clinical decision-making. papers.abstract_en: Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunohistochemistry, the current standard biomarker for predicting response to programmed death protein 1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors in non-small cell lung cancer, has moderate predictive value among others because of tumor heterogeneity and limited biopsy representation, whereas PD-L1 PET/CT using 18F-BMS-986192 enables noninvasive, whole-tumor assessment of PD-L1 expression and heterogeneity, potentially improving prediction of response to immunotherapy. Methods: In this prospective multicenter biomarker exploration study, patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer eligible for nivolumab-based therapies underwent baseline 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT, 18F-FDG PET/CT, and tumor biopsy for PD-L1 immunohistochemistry before treatment initiation. The primary endpoint was durable clinical benefit, defined as progression-free survival (PFS) of 9 mo or greater, with secondary analyses assessing associations among tracer uptake, PD-L1 expression, survival outcomes, and PET-based radiomic features. Results: Of 91 enrolled patients, 77 were included in the final analysis of 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT. Although PD-L1 immunohistochemistry did not differ between patients with PFS of less than 9 mo versus 9 mo or greater, PD-L1 PET uptake in lung lesions was significantly higher in patients with PFS of at least 9 mo (P = 0.01). Using an optimal mean SUVpeak cutoff of 2.4, PD-L1 PET demonstrated a high negative predictive value (94%) for durable clinical benefit, with significant associations for both PFS and overall survival, particularly in patients receiving first-line treatment. Tracer uptake showed no correlation with 18F-FDG uptake. Conclusion: 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT revealed interpatient PD-L1 variability. Low uptake in lung lesions predicted poor outcomes with high negative predictive value. 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT demonstrated stronger negative predictive value than did baseline PD-L1 immunohistochemistry in this cohort. These findings require prospective validation.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: The triglyceride high-density lipoprotein cholesterol-glucose body mass index (TyHGB) is a novel composite indicator integrating triglyceride, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, fasting glucose and body mass index and may provide a more comprehensive assessment of systemic metabolic status than current indices. This multicenter landmark cohort study aimed to determine the association between TyHGB measured at the landmark time and 28-day mortality in patients present in the intensive care units (ICUs) at that time and to evaluate its potential utility as a prognostic marker. METHODS: This multicenter observational cohort study included 1649 patients from 113 ICUs in China. The association between TyHGB and 28-day mortality was evaluated using three sequentially adjusted logistic regression models with restricted cubic splines: Model 1 adjusted for demographics; Model 2 further adjusted for disease severity and organ dysfunction; Model 3 additionally adjusted for therapeutic interventions. Subgroup analyses with interaction tests were conducted. Model performance was assessed by discrimination (AUC), calibration (Brier score and calibration slope) and internal validation via bootstrap resamples. RESULTS: Restricted cubic spline analysis demonstrated a positive association between TyHGB and 28-day mortality across fully adjusted models (P < 0.05). Subgroup analyses identified a statistically significant interaction with diabetes (P for interaction = 0.011). In the overall cohort, adding TyHGB to the base model improved AUC from 0.731 to 0.745 (ΔAUC = +0.014, P = 0.043), with significant improvements in reclassification (NRI = 0.328, P < 0.001; IDI = 0.012, P = 0.009) and model fit (LRT P < 0.001). Among diabetic patients (N = 401), TyHGB significantly improved AUC from 0.673 to 0.723 (ΔAUC = +0.050, P = 0.049; NRI = 0.515, P < 0.001; IDI = 0.041, P = 0.022). In contrast, no significant improvement was observed in non-diabetic patients (ΔAUC = +0.009, P = 0.152). CONCLUSION: Among patients present in participating ICUs at the landmark time, higher TyHGB was associated with subsequent 28-day mortality. However, adding TyHGB to the baseline risk prediction model led to only small improvements in overall predictive performance. Findings in diabetic patients are exploratory and require further validation.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Adherence to American Heart Association (AHA) ventilation guidelines during cardiac arrest is challenging. METHODS: Prospective, Before/After quality assurance study determining adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by Milwaukee County Emergency Medical Services and Kenosha Fire in Wisconsin using (Before) end tidal carbon dioxide [ETCO2] to monitor ventilations - Real BVM Help® applied but blinded versus (After) Real BVM Help®. PRIMARY ENDPOINTS: mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in-target for rate, tidal volume, and both rate and tidal volume. AHA 2020 guidelines were followed. RESULTS: From 9/29/22-12/22/23, 278 patients were entered (148 Before/130 After). Average age: 62.3±16.7 years; 185 (67%) male. Mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in Before/After Groups in-target for rate (47.7±25.1% vs 74.4±24.1% respectively, p<0.0001), tidal volume (15.3±15.4% vs 45.4±23.8% respectively, p<0.0001), and rate and tidal volume (7.5±9.6% vs 39.0±23.3% respectively, p<0.0001) were significantly higher in the After Group. In the Before Group, using ETCO2 to monitor all ventilations (N=22,037 ventilations), only 43.8% were in-target for rate, 13.5% in-target for tidal volume, and 6.8% in-target for rate and tidal volume with a lower-than-target tidal volume delivered in 58.2% of all ventilations. CONCLUSION: Real BVM Help® was associated with statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines. ETCO2 monitoring failed to approach both rate and tidal volume guideline adherence with a lower-than-target tidal volume being the most common parameter delivered out-of-target (58.2%). Ventilation rate and tidal volume monitoring with real-time feedback should be considered during treatment of cardiac arrest.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) after initial return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is associated with relatively poor outcomes. Early identification of rearrest might allow for intervention to prevent rearrest. In this study, we sought to determine whether clinical ECG features can predict rearrest. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients who achieved ROSC between 2018-2024. We evaluated the association of ECG features (QRS width, standard deviation of NN intervals, root mean square of successive NN interval differences, and percentage of NN intervals that differ by more than 50 milliseconds) within individual 15-second segments throughout a 5-minute window prior to rearrest as well as their temporal trends over the 5-minute analytic window. RESULTS: Of the 1,489 OHCA patients achieving ROSC, 1,298 were analyzed; 528 (40.7%) experienced rearrest. Rearrest patients were older, less likely to receive bystander CPR (48.7% vs. 61.9%), and had lower survival (20.4% vs. 43.1%) and favorable neurologic outcomes (7.8% vs. 21.2%; all p<0.001). We found lower heart rate, wider QRS, and higher HR variability in those with rearrest. Identification was highest 1 minute prior to rearrest (AUROC 0.74), declining beyond 3 minutes. Models using temporal trends achieved AUROC 0.67; strongest predictors were heart rate variability measures and QRS width. CONCLUSION: Established ECG features achieved good prediction for rearrest with identification improving closer to time of rearrest. Future work leveraging novel features or more advanced artificial intelligence models may further improve prediction.
