papers.abstract_en: Somalia's health system is a fragmented mixed market. Private for-profit and not-for-profit providers deliver most curative care, external donors finance most health spending, and the instruments needed to regulate this market remain largely in draft or unenforced. National plans set out what the system should deliver, but they say less about how leaders and managers should run organizations and purchasing arrangements within such a market. This evidence-informed policy commentary addresses that gap. It is not a systematic review: sources were selected purposively by the author from peer-reviewed literature and from official Somali, World Health Organization, and World Bank Group-supported reports, without a protocol-driven search or formal quality appraisal. From these sources the author proposes an eight-pillar conceptual framework: public stewardship of the healthcare market; accountable public-private partnerships; value-based management; sustainable healthcare financing; a national quality and accreditation system; digital and managerial innovation; procurement and supply-chain reform; and leadership and the healthcare workforce. The central argument is that leadership and stewardship capacity, more than the number of providers, is the binding constraint, and that management instruments borrowed from business strategy help only when they are sequenced behind that capacity and kept subordinate to equity, quality, and patient safety. The pillars largely reorganize established health-system strengthening principles; the contribution lies in linking each to a documented Somali problem, a leadership requirement, and a feasibility condition. The framework is author-generated and has not been validated through stakeholder consultation, costing, or empirical testing, and the evidence for several of its instruments, including contracting, performance-based payment, and community-based insurance, is mixed. It should therefore be read as a set of policy considerations for consultation, piloting, and evaluation, not as a demonstrated solution.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Autoimmune glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) astrocytopathy is a rare autoimmune inflammatory disease of the central nervous system that frequently mimics infectious meningoencephalitis. Because its clinical presentation, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings, and inflammatory markers often resemble central nervous system infection, diagnosis may be delayed, postponing appropriate immunotherapy. CASE PRESENTATION: We describe two women with markedly different clinical presentations of GFAP astrocytopathy who were initially managed as suspected infectious meningoencephalitis. Both patients presented with inflammatory CSF findings, negative extensive microbiological investigations, and initial empirical antimicrobial treatment. In the first case, persistent aseptic meningitis with recurrent symptoms prompted autoimmune testing after repeated negative infectious work-up. In the second case, rapidly progressive encephalopathy requiring intensive care initially suggested severe infectious meningoencephalitis. In both patients, neuronal surface and paraneoplastic antibody testing was negative, whereas indirect immunofluorescence detected GFAP-IgG, supporting the diagnosis in the context of the clinical, CSF, neuroimaging, and microbiological findings. Both patients subsequently received corticosteroid treatment and experienced clinical improvement, although residual neurological symptoms persisted in the first patient. CONCLUSION: These cases highlight the broad clinical spectrum of GFAP astrocytopathy and its potential to closely mimic infectious central nervous system disease. Earlier recognition of GFAP astrocytopathy may facilitate timely consideration of immunotherapy and help reduce diagnostic delay and unnecessary antimicrobial exposure in patients with inflammatory meningoencephalitic presentations and negative infectious investigations.

papers.abstract_en: Chemical synapses are fundamental computational units of the nervous system that enable rapid and precise information transfer through the nanoscale organization of presynaptic and postsynaptic components. Despite hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution and extraordinary diversity in nervous system architectures, the core physiological principles of chemical synaptic transmission remain remarkably conserved. Studies across Drosophila melanogaster, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, frogs and mammals reveal recurring principles governing active-zone organization, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, calcium signalling and postsynaptic specialization. Here, we examine the evolution of chemical synapses across the animal kingdom, focusing on the relationship between molecular diversification, nanoscale organization and functional conservation. We propose that the evolutionary stability of synapses reflects, in part, a stringent biophysical constraint imposed by the requirements for rapid chemical communication. We further consider how these conserved synaptic operations are assembled into neural circuits of dramatically different complexities, as well as the ctenophore nervous system as a critical test case for distinguishing molecular conservation from architectural and functional convergence. Across species, the emerging picture is that evolution has adhered to conserving the geometry and organizational principles of chemical synapses more stringently than a precise molecular composition. Synapses thus represent stable yet adaptable information-processing architectures in which conserved nanoscale constraints coexist with molecular flexibility and extensive diversification of neural circuits.
